Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner Outbound to GitHub Gist (tj-actions CVE-2025-30066)
id: 6f2a1c84-9d3e-4f7a-b0c1-2e5a8d4f9b31
description: A GitHub Actions runner-context process connecting to gist.githubusercontent.com, matching the second-stage payload fetch of the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action.
references:

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

10 Layers Deep: How StepSecurity Stops TeamPCP's Trivy Supply Chain Attack on GitHub Actions

StepSecurity
2026-07-02 8 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

TeamPCP weaponized 76 Trivy version tags overnight. The KICS attack followed the same playbook days later. One security control is not enough. Here is how the StepSecurity platform's ten independent security layers work together to prevent credential exfiltration, detect compromised actions at runtime, and respond to incidents across your entire organization before attackers can succeed.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner spawns network tool / interpreter under compromised trivy-action or KICS · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 · [LLM] DNS resolution of TeamPCP typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker
TeamPCP Trivy/KICS supply-chain credential exfil to scan.aquasecurtiy.org & 45.148.10.212 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from CI/CD runners (or any onboarded host) to the exact exfiltration infrastructure used by TeamPCP's compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action and Checkmarx KICS actions. Any egress to these hard IOCs means the credential stealer's POST reached the wire. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim exfil host scan.aquasecurtiy.org (typosquat resolving to 45.148.10.212) plus the pre-extracted secondary IOC IPs/domains; connection to any is near-zero-FP and confirms secrets left the runner.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher deliberately detonating the compromised action in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving/probing the IOC domains
  • A blocked/failed connection logged by a proxy that never actually exfiltrated
  • Internal typosquat-monitoring service crawling lookalike domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/runner and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; confirm whether it is a CI runner that recently executed aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets/tokens exposed to that job (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC creds, registry creds) and revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: pull every repo/workflow that referenced the compromised action across the org, pivot on the /proc/pid/mem credential-harvest UC, and block the IOC IPs/domains at egress.

Credential harvest via /proc/<pid>/mem read of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core TeamPCP payload behaviour: a spawned interpreter (python/node/sh) reading /proc/<pid>/mem of the Runner.Worker process to scrape marked secrets from runner memory. This is the article's exact credential-access primitive, independent of the exfil endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact TTP — a payload process reading /proc/pid/mem of the Runner.Worker process — as the pivot; the Runner.Worker parent + interpreter + /proc/*/mem triad is specific to CI runner memory-scraping and rarely legitimate.
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate profiling/debugging tools (gdb, py-spy) attached to a runner job by a maintainer
  • Crash-dump or coredump collection tooling reading /proc during a CI failure
  • Custom self-hosted-runner health scripts inspecting worker memory usage
  • Security agents themselves reading /proc for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","gdb","coredumpctl","/usr/bin/perf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the target PID; confirm the parent is the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker and the child interpreter is not part of the declared workflow. 2) Contain: kill the job, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret injected into that workflow run plus any downstream cloud OIDC tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2 egress UC (scan.aquasecurtiy.org/45.148.10.212) within the same job window, and enumerate all repos referencing aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS by tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker" or ProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","sh","bash","perl","ruby")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "mem"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape via /proc/pid/mem
id: c1d4e7a2-5b62-4f18-8a90-77e3b1c2f6d0
description: Detects an interpreter spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process reading /proc/<pid>/mem to extract secrets from runner memory, matching TeamPCP's trivy-action credential stealer.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1003.007
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains: 'Runner.Worker'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/proc/'
      - 'mem'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(python OR python3 OR node OR bash OR sh OR perl OR ruby) (@process.command_line:*"/proc/"* AND @process.command_line:*mem*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/Runner\.Worker/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(python3?|node|bash|sh|perl|ruby)$/i
| regex("/proc/", field=CommandLine)
| regex("mem", field=CommandLine)

DNS resolution of TeamPCP typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups for the misspelled typosquat scan.aquasecurtiy.org (impersonating aquasecurity) and the other TeamPCP staging/exfil domains. Catches the campaign at name-resolution even when egress is blocked or the C2 IP rotates. Rationale: The domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org is an intentional typosquat of aquasecurity called out verbatim in the article; resolving it (or the other named TeamPCP domains) is a high-fidelity, rotation-resistant signal that survives IP changes.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typosquat-monitoring / brand-protection service resolving lookalike domains
  • Malware sandbox or IOC-validation pipeline resolving the domains
  • Passive-DNS collector or threat-intel feed enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole logging the query after redirect
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and the initiating process; determine if it is a CI runner mid-workflow vs a research/monitoring system. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains org-wide, isolate the runner, and rotate secrets scoped to any workflow that ran on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the resolved IP against the C2-connection UC, and check whether the /proc/pid/mem harvest fired on the same host within the job window.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Actions runner spawns network tool / interpreter under compromised trivy-action or KICS AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the execution stage of the supply-chain payload: the Runner.Worker (or a trivy/kics action step) spawning curl/wget/python/node that then reaches the internet — the shape a weaponized aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS tag exhibits when it stages/exfils. Rationale: Grounds on the article's named compromised actions (aquasecurity/trivy-action, Checkmarx KICS) and the Runner.Worker process; a scanner action shelling out to curl/wget/python for outbound POSTs is off-pattern for legitimate SCA/SBOM tooling.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate trivy DB update fetching vulnerability feeds via curl/wget over HTTPS
  • A workflow step that legitimately uses python/node to post results to an internal dashboard
  • Self-hosted runner bootstrap scripts pulling dependencies
  • Container image scan steps that curl a registry manifest
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aquasec.com","ghcr.io","github.com","trivy-db","vulnerability-db") and not ProcessCommandLine has "scan.aquasecurtiy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the ChildProcessCommandLine destination — is it an official aquasecurity/checkmarx endpoint or an unknown/typosquat host? Cross-check the action tag/ref used against the known-compromised list. 2) Contain: cancel the run, isolate the runner, rotate secrets exposed to the job, and pin/replace the action to a verified SHA. 3) Hunt: correlate to the C2, DNS, and /proc/pid/mem UCs on the same host+job, and org-wide enumerate every workflow referencing the compromised action by mutable tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("trivy","trivy-action","kics")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","-d ","--data","POST","/proc/","scan.aquasecurtiy")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("trivy","trivy-action","kics")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","nc","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","--data","POST","/proc/","scan.aquasecurtiy")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

9router API key / secret exfiltration via /api/settings/database without prior login AIActions on Objectives Medium
After forging a session cookie, the attacker reads stored provider API keys and auth tokens from 9router's /api/settings/database endpoint. This correlates access to the settings/secret endpoints against the source ever having performed a successful POST /api/auth/login — a forged-token holder never logs in, so absence of a login is the tell. Rationale: Targets the article's named exfiltration path /api/settings/database ("steal valuable API Key, Auth Token") and the operational fact that a forged cookie bypasses the login flow entirely — so a leftanti against successful POST /api/auth/login isolates forged sessions. Sigma/Datadog/Defender/Falcon empty: this is a multi-event correlation on web-tier logs, not a single-event or endpoint signal. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-49352/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jphh-m39h-6gwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin session where the login POST landed outside the lookback window or was logged by a different proxy node (login not observed for that src)
  • Automation / IaC that reads 9router settings using a long-lived valid cookie and never re-authenticates in-window
  • Shared NAT egress where one user logged in and another admin IP-shares the same source address
  • Health-check or config-backup jobs polling /api/settings
Suppression filter
// Exclude known automation egress IPs that legitimately read settings with a persistent session:
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.20.0.15", "10.20.0.16")   // replace with your config-management egress IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request sequence for the SrcIpAddr; confirm the auth_token cookie matches the forged shape from UC1 and that no successful /api/auth/login exists for it across all proxy nodes. Check HTTP status on /api/settings/database (200 = secrets returned). 2) CONTAIN: Rotate ALL provider API keys and auth tokens held by 9router immediately (treat as disclosed), set JWT_SECRET + restart, block the source IP. 3) HUNT: Check for password-change and shutdown API calls from the same source, and for outbound use of the stolen keys against upstream provider APIs (billing/usage spikes).
let Lookback = 7d;
let LoggedIn = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where HttpMethod == "POST"
    | where Url has "/api/auth/login"
    | where HttpStatusCode between (200 .. 299)
    | distinct SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database" or Url has "/api/settings"
| where HttpRequestHeaderCookie has "auth_token="
| where SrcIpAddr !in (LoggedIn)     // forged-token holder never authenticated
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderCookie
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" OR Web.uri_path="*/api/settings*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=left src [ | tstats `summariesonly` count as login_count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/api/auth/login*" Web.http_method=POST (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=204) by Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where isnull(login_count)
| sort - lastTime
| table firstTime lastTime src dest uri_path http_method status
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" OR Web.uri_path="*/api/settings*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.uri_path Web.http_method Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=left src [ | tstats summariesonly=false count as login_count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/api/auth/login*" Web.http_method=POST (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=204) by Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where isnull(login_count)
| sort - lastTime
| table firstTime lastTime src dest uri_path http_method status
9router unauthenticated MCP / cli-tools route RCE via process spawn — CVE-2026-46339 AIExploitation Medium
The 9router middleware only guards 8 routes, leaving /api/mcp/* and /api/cli-tools/* (40+ routes, added in v0.4.30) with no authentication, allowing unauthenticated OS command execution as the 9router user. Detects both the inbound requests to those routes and the resulting node process spawning a shell/interpreter child on the host. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route prefixes named in the CVE-2026-46339 write-up (/api/mcp/*, /api/cli-tools/*, unguarded since v0.4.30) for the web tier, and the RCE's on-host signature (the node process spawning a shell) for EDR. Corroborated via the GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj advisory and Endor Labs' analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-46339
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authorized use of the 9router MCP stdio->SSE bridge invoking a local tool that spawns a helper process
  • node-based build tooling / npm scripts on a shared dev box spawning sh/bash (scope the EDR rule to the 9router server to remove this)
  • MCP plugin health-checks or self-tests that shell out
  • Monitoring agents that proxy /api/mcp/ readiness probes
Suppression filter
// EDR side: scope to the 9router install path once known, to strip generic node->shell dev noise:
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("9router", "node_modules\\9router")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the /api/mcp/ or /api/cli-tools/ request time against the node->shell spawn on the same host; inspect ProcessCommandLine / InitiatingProcessCommandLine for attacker commands (whoami, curl, base64, reverse-shell). Confirm 9router version is 0.4.30-0.4.36 (unpatched for CVE-2026-46339). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, upgrade 9router to >=0.4.45, and restrict /api/mcp/ + /api/cli-tools/ at the proxy/WAF. 3) HUNT: Sweep for persistence and outbound C2 from the node process (DeviceNetworkEvents / NetworkConnectIP4 with ContextImageFileName node), dropped files, and reuse of the same source IP against other exposed 9router hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/mcp/" or Url has "/api/cli-tools/"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderCookie
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GravitLauncher LaunchServer secret read via unauth path traversal (ecdsa_id/legacySalt/LaunchServer.json) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the LaunchServer file server that reference the server's own secret files outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, .keys/rsa_id, .keys/legacySalt, LaunchServer.json). A successful read of ecdsa_id hands the attacker the JWT signing key, yielding a full admin auth bypass, so any such request is high-fidelity regardless of traversal encoding. Rationale: Uses the exact secret filenames the advisory names as readable outside updatesDir (.keys/ecdsa_id, rsa_id, legacySalt, LaunchServer.json) — legitimate GravitLauncher clients only fetch update payloads under updatesDir and never reference these, so any hit is near-certainly exploitation of CVE-2026-54617. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) running a CVE-2026-54617 template against the LaunchServer host
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement replaying the PoC
  • An update artifact legitimately named LaunchServer.json placed inside updatesDir and requested by a client
  • Security researcher probing the public 9274 endpoint after the CVE disclosure
  • Backup/monitoring tooling misconfigured to fetch config files over the file-server port
Suppression filter
| where DeviceProduct != "VulnScanner" and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0")  // exclude the sanctioned scanner subnet / host once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line and HTTP status for the source IP — a 200/OK with a non-zero body means the secret bytes were actually served (compromise); a 404 means the safe leading-slash branch was hit. Note whether the target was ecdsa_id/legacySalt (auth bypass) or LaunchServer.json (DB creds). 2) Contain: firewall port 9274 to internal only or rebind LaunchServer to 127.0.0.1; treat the ECDSA signing key, legacySalt and DB credentials as compromised and rotate all three immediately, invalidating outstanding JWTs. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP look for follow-on `../../../../etc/passwd`-style reads, and pivot to authentication logs for anomalous admin-account token use or DB logins from new IPs after the read timestamp.
let LaunchServerSecrets = dynamic(["ecdsa_id","rsa_id",".keys","legacySalt","LaunchServer.json"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any (LaunchServerSecrets)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LaunchServer path-traversal exploit signature: request-target without leading slash / %2e%2e on port 9274 AIExploitation High
Hunts the structural exploitation signature of CVE-2026-54617 — an HTTP request-target that does NOT begin with '/' (e.g. 'GET ../../.keys/ecdsa_id') or uses '%2e%2e' encoding, aimed at the default 0.0.0.0:9274 file-server bind. This catches depth-robust arbitrary-file reads (../../../../etc/passwd) that the secret-filename query would miss, since only the no-leading-slash form escapes updatesDir. Rationale: Keys on the advisory's unique root-cause signature: only a request-target lacking a leading slash (or %2e%2e-encoded) escapes updatesDir, while curl/browsers/normal clients always prepend '/'. Port 9274 is the article's default 0.0.0.0 bind; the Defender/Falcon clauses only give coarse public-inbound-to-9274 exposure because FDR/AH carry no HTTP URI. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g75-477j-2c2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/pro.gravit.launcher/launchserver-api/CVE-2026-54617/
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner firing generic '../' and '%2e%2e' path-traversal payloads at the endpoint
  • Misbehaving HTTP client or crawler emitting a relative (non-absolute) request-target
  • Legitimate query-string parameter that happens to contain '../' being logged in RequestURL
  • Load-balancer / L4 health-check tooling hitting 9274 with non-standard request lines
  • Defender/Falcon exposure clause alone: any benign public connection to 9274 (this clause is exposure, not exploitation)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "../" and RequestURL !startswith ".." and RequestURL !has "%2e%2e")  // keep only the no-leading-slash / encoded form, drop benign embedded ../ in query strings
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request-target genuinely lacks a leading slash or uses %2e%2e (the exploit form) versus a normal '/..' that the server 404s; check the HTTP status and byte count to see if a file was served. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the L4 firewall and restrict 9274 to trusted management ranges or rebind to 127.0.0.1; a normalizing L7 proxy in front returns 400 for these — deploy or enforce one. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct traversal target from that IP (etc/passwd, .keys/*, LaunchServer.json) to gauge what was read, and if any secret was served, rotate the ECDSA key/legacySalt/DB creds and audit downstream JWT and DB activity.

| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName

| order by TimeGenerated desc

fast-mcp-telegram traversal token in request URL (URL-auth middleware) CVE-2026-52830 AIExploitation High
Hunts the URL-auth variant of CVE-2026-52830 where the traversal token is carried in the request path/query rather than the Authorization header. Surfaces web access-log requests to a fast-mcp-telegram server whose URI contains '../fast-mcp-telegram/telegram', %2e%2e-encoded traversal, or a direct telegram.session reference. Rationale: Pivots on the URL field instead of the Authorization header (the article calls out both header auth and URL auth, and URL-encoded traversal 'if any route decodes path components'), using the same concrete CVE strings so it catches deployments that log full URIs but strip auth headers. Unauthenticated POST to 9router /api/tunnel/tailscale-install (CVE-2026-59800 auth bypass) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the 9router route /api/tunnel/tailscale-install, which is absent from the dashboard middleware matcher and therefore reaches the handler with no cookie/JWT/CLI-token check. Any external hit on this endpoint is an exploitation attempt for the unauthenticated RCE, since this route is only ever driven by the local dashboard. Rationale: The exact route path /api/tunnel/tailscale-install and its absence from the src/proxy.js matcher are the article's core auth-bypass fact; any POST to it is exploitation. Defender query surfaces external hosts reaching the 9router listener on port 20128 (EXPOSE 20128 in the PoC) as a supporting exposure signal since Defender lacks L7 URI visibility. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59800
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized operator installing Tailscale through the 9router dashboard UI (request originates from localhost/loopback, not a public IP)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing the CVE-2026-59800 endpoint
  • Automated uptime/health monitor mis-configured to POST to the tunnel path
  • Security team running the published PoC in a sanctioned test
  • DAST/CI security pipeline exercising the API surface
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/non-loopback and capture the full request; check whether the 9router host runs Node as root (docker inspect / systemd unit User=) which turns this into remote root. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy, take the 9router instance offline or restrict /api/tunnel/* at the reverse proxy, and upgrade 9router to >=0.4.44. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host for node->sudo -S sh spawns and curl fetches of tailscale.com/install.sh in the seconds after the POST to determine if code executed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 20128
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","9router") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "9router"
| summarize Conns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(LocalPort) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Conns desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/tunnel/tailscale-install"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router (node) process spawning 'sudo -S sh' — CVE-2026-59800 command injection primitive AIExploitation High
Detects the 9router Node process spawning 'sudo -S sh', the exact child process the vulnerable installTailscaleLinux routine creates and into whose stdin the attacker-controlled sudoPassword is written. A Node/9router parent spawning a password-fed root shell is the execution primitive of the RCE. Rationale: 'sudo -S sh' spawned by a node/9router parent is taken verbatim from installTailscaleLinux in src/lib/tunnel/tailscale.js; the -S flag (read password from stdin) plus a Node parent is the article-specific fingerprint distinguishing this from interactive sudo use. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated Tailscale install triggered through the 9router dashboard (same code path, benign stdin)
  • Other Node apps that legitimately shell out via 'sudo -S sh' with a cached password
  • Automation/CI runner that pipes install scripts through sudo -S
  • Config-management tooling wrapping sudo shells under a Node supervisor
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and the children of the sh process — a legitimate install shows apt-get/curl/tailscaled; injection shows recon (id/whoami), file writes to /tmp, or network tools, and Tailscale never actually installs. Check InitiatingProcessId lineage back to the 9router listener. 2) Contain: kill the node/sh process tree, isolate the host, rotate any secrets reachable as the 9router user (root if containerized), upgrade to >=0.4.44. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (a preceding unauthenticated POST) and UC3 (curl fetch of tailscale.com/install.sh) within the same PID lineage; sweep other 9router hosts for the same node->sudo->sh pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "sudo"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S","sh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","9router") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "9router"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "sudo"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_all ("-S","sh")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs","9router") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "9router"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessId, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router chain: node fetches tailscale.com/install.sh then spawns sudo -S sh within seconds AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-stage exploitation chain: the 9router Node process spawning curl/wget to fetch https://tailscale.com/install.sh, immediately followed (same parent PID, <=10s) by a 'sudo -S sh' spawn. Tying both events to the same node parent PID confirms the CVE-2026-59800 fetch-then-pipe-to-root-shell sequence rather than either half in isolation. Rationale: Both the curl fetch of tailscale.com/install.sh and the sudo -S sh spawn are the exact code path in tailscale.js; joining on the shared node parent PID within seconds captures the full attack chain and drops either half occurring alone, giving a low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized Tailscale install via the 9router dashboard executes the identical fetch+sudo sequence (benign) — treat as TP-worthy only when no authorized change window matches
  • Operator manually re-running the install through the app during troubleshooting
  • Blue-team detonation of the CVE PoC in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the fetch and sudo events share the node parent PID and occurred within seconds; inspect whether the sh child ran install.sh's expected commands or exited early (the '; exit 0' injection kills sh before tailscaled installs). Check for a preceding unauthenticated POST (UC1). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, rotate credentials accessible to the 9router/root user, upgrade to >=0.4.44. 3) Hunt: enumerate all children spawned by the sh process for dropped files, reverse shells, or new persistence; sweep the fleet for other 9router hosts exhibiting the same fetch->sudo chain.

    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("curl","wget")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "tailscale.com/install.sh"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","9router") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "9router"
    | project FetchTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, NodeParentId = InitiatingProcessId, FetchCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents

| order by SudoTime desc

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

curl/wget child of 9router node fetching tailscale.com/install.sh (probe or exploit delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Flags the outbound fetch of tailscale.com/install.sh by a curl/wget process whose parent is the 9router Node process. Per the advisory, this fetch fires on every hit to the endpoint — including hardened hosts where the sudo step later fails — so it surfaces both successful exploitation and reconnaissance/probing of CVE-2026-59800. Rationale: The article states the endpoint always triggers 'an outbound fetch from tailscale.com' even when RCE fails, making curl/wget->tailscale.com/install.sh with a node parent a reliable probe indicator; parent=node distinguishes it from a human running the official install command in a shell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59800
ATT&CKT1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized Tailscale install through the 9router dashboard (parent is genuinely node and the fetch is legitimate)
  • Administrator running the official 'curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh' from a shell (parent would be bash/sh, excluded by the node-parent filter)
  • Container image build step pre-installing Tailscale under a node entrypoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","9router")
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine if a matching unauthenticated POST (UC1) preceded the fetch and whether a sudo -S sh spawn (UC2/UC3) followed on the same host/PID — fetch-only with no sudo success suggests a probe against a hardened host. 2) Contain: if paired with sudo execution, isolate and treat as compromise; otherwise restrict /api/tunnel/* at the proxy and prioritize the upgrade to >=0.4.44. 3) Hunt: aggregate source IPs of the inbound POSTs across all 9router hosts to identify a scanning campaign (Shadowserver reported in-the-wild exploitation from 2026-07-04).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "tailscale.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","9router")
| summarize Fetches = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by Fetches desc

Web-server process writes PHP file into Mautic config/cache/media/logs (zip-slip landing) AIInstallation High
Hunts the core of CVE-2026-9559: the Mautic campaign-import ZIP extraction escaping the temp directory and dropping an attacker-controlled .php/.phtml/.phar into Symfony's config, var/cache, var/logs or media trees, executed under the web-server user (php-fpm/apache/nginx). A web-server process writing executable PHP into these directories at request time is almost never legitimate outside a controlled cache warm-up. Rationale: Keys on the article's concrete outcome — 'write arbitrary PHP files to sensitive system directories … overwrite critical internal configuration or cache components' — using Mautic 7's real Symfony layout (config/, var/cache, var/logs, media) plus the web-server process identity that owns the write. Corroborated against NVD and the Mautic 7.1.2 release; the Symfony compiled-container exclusion removes the one high-volume legitimate PHP-into-cache writer. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-6r9h-4h75-7q4x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9559 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9559/ • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/releases/tag/7.1.2
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Symfony cache warm-up writing compiled container/service PHP into /var/cache/prod/ on first request or after `bin/console cache:clear`
  • Mautic plugin/theme installation via the admin UI writing PHP assets into media or plugin dirs
  • In-place Mautic upgrade / Composer operation regenerating cached PHP
  • Backup-restore tooling repopulating var/cache from a snapshot
  • Developer or deploy script running as the web user during a controlled release window
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/var/cache/" and (FileName startswith "Container" or FileName endswith "ProjectContainer.php" or FileName startswith "srcApp_Kernel" or FileName matches regex @"get[A-Za-z0-9_]+Service\.php$")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cache:warmup","cache:clear","assets:install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the exact FolderPath/FileName and SHA256, and read the dropped file — attacker webshells contain eval/system/base64_decode/assert; legitimate Symfony cache files are compiled container/service classes. Confirm whether a campaign import ran on this host within the prior 5 minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the Mautic host or block inbound HTTP; quarantine the dropped PHP; revoke campaign:imports:create from all non-admin users and rotate the app secret/DB creds if the file is a shell. 3) Hunt: pivot on the web-server user for subsequent shell spawns and outbound connections, enumerate every .php written under config/var/cache/var/logs/media in the last 30 days, and confirm the instance is patched to Mautic 7.1.2.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".pht" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/config/","/var/cache/","/var/logs/","/media/")
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php-fpm" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php","php8"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
// drop Symfony's legitimate compiled-container cache writes
| where not (FolderPath has "/var/cache/" and (FileName startswith "Container" or FileName endswith "ProjectContainer.php" or FileName startswith "srcApp_Kernel"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","phar","pht","php5","php7")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/","/var/cache/","/var/logs/","/media/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where not (TargetFilePath has "/var/cache/" and (TargetFileName startswith "Container" or TargetFileName endswith "ProjectContainer.php" or TargetFileName startswith "srcApp_Kernel"))

Mautic campaign import ZIP upload — POST to campaign import endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the delivery step of CVE-2026-9559: an authenticated POST to the Mautic campaign-import route carrying the malicious ZIP. Hunting-tier because import is a legitimate feature; pivot on the source user/IP and correlate against a PHP file-write (UC1) on the same host within ~60s to promote to a confirmed exploit. Rationale: Grounded on the article's named privilege/feature (campaign:imports:create, 'campaign import feature', ZIP upload) confirmed as a Mautic 7 REST feature accepting ZIP form-data. Alone it is a legitimate action, so it is scoped as a hunt whose value is the source-actor pivot and correlation with UC1's PHP write. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-6r9h-4h75-7q4x • https://devdocs.mautic.org/en/5.x/rest_api/campaigns.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9559/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing admin legitimately importing a campaign template exported from another Mautic instance
  • Migration/onboarding project bulk-importing campaigns during a cutover window
  • CI/CD or IaC tooling restoring campaign definitions from a repo
  • Vendor/consultant importing a packaged campaign bundle
  • Automated backup-restore re-importing campaign archives
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SrcUsername/SrcIpAddr and check whether this account has ever performed a campaign import before and whether campaign:imports:create was recently granted; verify the source IP is within the IT-admin/marketing range. 2) Contain: if the actor is new/unexpected, disable the account, revoke campaign:imports:create org-wide, and preserve the uploaded ZIP for analysis. 3) Hunt: correlate this import timestamp against UC1 PHP file-writes on the Mautic host within 60s and against any web-server shell spawn; if a drop is found, treat as confirmed RCE and escalate.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "campaigns/import" or Url has "campaign/import"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request to an executable PHP file under Mautic /media (web-shell interaction) AICommand & Control High
Detects the execution/command channel after CVE-2026-9559: an HTTP request that reaches a .php/.phtml/.phar under Mautic's web-accessible /media path (which should only ever serve static assets) and returns 200, indicating the dropped web shell was invoked. Distinct pivot from the file-write (UC1) — this fires on the web-access log even if endpoint telemetry is absent. Rationale: The article's RCE outcome lands PHP into config/cache/media; only /media is web-reachable, and Mautic serves it as a static-asset store, so any PHP under /media returning 200 is a web-shell invocation — a clean, high-fidelity signal that needs no threshold. Scoped to 200/500 to drop scanner 404 noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-6r9h-4h75-7q4x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9559 • https://securityonline.info/mautic-security-vulnerabilities-rce/

  • Developer leaving a phpinfo/test file in media during troubleshooting
  • WAF or CDN health-check hitting an asset URL that happens to include .php in a query string
  • Misrouted request where .php appears only in the query parameter, not the path (regex anchors on path extension to avoid this)

Mautic Twig SSTI RCE: PHP/web process spawns OS shell (CVE-2026-9558) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation observable of CVE-2026-9558 — a Mautic web-tier process (php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd/nginx worker, or w3wp) directly spawning an interactive shell or recon binary. In a healthy Mautic install the PHP runtime never forks /bin/sh or whoami; when it does, an uploaded Twig theme has broken the sandbox and reached OS-command execution. Rationale: Grounded in Mautic's confirmed PHP/Symfony/Twig stack (advisory + GitLab/NVD) — the vuln renders theme Twig without a sandbox, so successful exploitation manifests as the PHP runtime forking a shell, which never happens in a benign Mautic web request. Parent(php/apache/nginx/w3wp)->child(shell/recon) is the highest-fidelity RCE pivot available without article-supplied hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9558 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/mautic-critical-ssti-cve-2026-9558-allows-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mautic scheduled tasks (php bin/console mautic:segments:update / mautic:emails:send) spawning sh for symfony process helpers
  • Composer/deployment scripts run as the web user invoking shell hooks during an upgrade
  • PDF/preview generation plugins shelling out to wkhtmltopdf or imagemagick's convert
  • Admin using a web-based file manager or terminal plugin on the same PHP-FPM pool
  • Monitoring/backup agents that exec via the PHP-FPM worker (e.g. New Relic, healthcheck shellouts)
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has "bin/console" or ChildCmd has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","wkhtmltoimage","convert -","composer") or ParentCmd has "bin/console")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — a legit Symfony console task references 'bin/console'; an attacker command runs whoami/id/curl to an external host or reads /etc/passwd or Mautic's app/config/local.php. Confirm the acting host runs Mautic and check its version against 7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke sessions/API tokens for any Mautic user holding core:themes:create; block outbound to any C2 seen in the child cmdline. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for UC2 (new .twig under themes/), review Mautic audit log for recent theme installs, and sweep for dropped web shells or cron persistence written by the PHP user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "php" or ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","cmd.exe","powershell","whoami","/id","uname","curl","wget","python","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponized Twig theme written under Mautic themes/ by web process (CVE-2026-9558) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the delivery step of CVE-2026-9558 — the Mautic web tier (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) writing a .twig template into the themes/ directory, i.e. an uploaded/created theme landing on disk. Pairs with the RCE detection: a fresh web-written theme template followed by a PHP-spawned shell on the same host is the full SSTI chain. Rationale: Mautic docs confirm themes are self-contained dirs under themes/ holding *.html.twig files, installed by uploading a zip through the web UI — so the payload physically lands as a web-process-written .twig. Scoping the writer to the PHP/web runtime (not an admin's editor) separates exploit-driven writes from developer file edits and gives a clean pivot to correlate with the UC1 shell spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://docs.mautic.org/en/5.2/builders/creating_themes.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator installing or updating a theme zip via Settings > Themes
  • Mautic version upgrade repopulating bundled themes (blank, cards, nature, etc.) into themes/
  • Marketing/design team uploading a custom corporate email/page theme
  • CI/CD or deployment automation syncing theme directories as the web user
  • Theme builder saving edits to email.html.twig / page.html.twig from the UI
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which Mautic user triggered the write via the app audit log (Settings > Audit Log) and correlate the timestamp with the FolderPath; a new theme folder name you don't recognize, or a modified base/page/email .twig on an internet-facing host, is suspicious. Grab and read the .twig content for SSTI markers (_self.env, registerUndefinedFilterCallback, getFilter, system/exec/passthru/proc_open). 2) Contain: quarantine the theme file, revoke core:themes:create from the acting user pending review, and confirm the host is on a patched build (7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20). 3) Hunt: run UC1 on the same DeviceName for a php-spawned shell within minutes of the write, and review web/access logs for the theme-install POST and subsequent theme-preview/render requests.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/themes/" and FileName endswith ".twig"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/themes/" and TargetFileName endswith ".twig"
| where ActingProcessName has "php" or ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Affected zebrad (<= v4.4.1) exposure to P2SH sigop consensus-split (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts with an installed Zebra/zebrad build at or below v4.4.1, which undercounts P2SH sigops and can be forced into a chain split from zcashd. This is asset-exposure hunting: identify vulnerable Zcash full nodes before an attacker broadcasts malicious P2SH-spend transactions. Rationale: Uses the concrete affected boundary from the advisory (zebrad <= v4.4.1, patched in 4.4.2) and CVE-2026-52735. parse_version gives an exact vulnerable-version test; SoftwareName 'zebrad' avoids collision with unrelated Zebra Technologies printer software. Note: GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 later found the 4.4.2 fix incomplete, so 4.5.1 is the true-safe floor. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/ • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 • https://dailycve.com/zebra-consensus-divergence-critical/

Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities

  • Decommissioned or lab-only Zcash test nodes that never touch mainnet consensus
  • Host already upgraded but vuln scanner holding a stale software-inventory record
  • Vulnerability scanner mis-mapping a different Zebra advisory to this CVE

| where SoftwareVendor !has "Zebra Technologies" and SoftwareName !has "printer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually runs a validating full node (not just an installed binary) and note the exact SoftwareVersion — anything < 4.4.2 is exposed to CVE-2026-52735. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to a patched build; because the 4.4.2 fix was found incomplete (GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443), upgrade straight to >= 4.5.1. Until patched, monitor the node's chain tip against a reference zcashd node for divergence. 3) Hunt: enumerate all zebrad hosts via inventory, and pivot to UC 'zebrad node process execution' and the 'bad-blk-sigops' log hunt to see whether an exploit block was already accepted.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "zebrad" or (SoftwareVendor has "Zcash" and SoftwareName has "zebra")
| where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
| where parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")   // 4.4.2 = first patched build per CVE-2026-52735
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-52735" or (SoftwareName has "zebrad" and parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

zebrad node process execution at vulnerable version (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts live execution of the zebrad binary and surfaces its product version so analysts can confirm exposure to the P2SH sigop-undercount consensus split. Complements inventory-based detection by catching nodes launched from non-packaged paths (source builds, containers) that TVM may miss. Rationale: Anchors on the exact binary name 'zebrad' from the advisory and surfaces ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion so analysts can read the version off Windows builds; Linux builds (no version info) are still surfaced rather than dropped. Distinct pivot from the TVM inventory UC — catches source/container launches inventory misses. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate zebrad node operators running an already-patched build (>= 4.5.1) — version column disambiguates on Windows
  • CI/CD or automated test harnesses repeatedly spawning zebrad
  • Container orchestration restarting zebrad pods (high event volume, benign)
  • Linux hosts where product-version metadata is empty, forcing manual version confirmation
Suppression filter
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion; if empty (typical on Linux), query the node RPC/`zebrad --version` to get the build. Versions < 4.4.2 are exposed. 2) Contain: for exposed validating nodes, plan upgrade to >= 4.5.1 (the 4.4.2 patch was incomplete) and watch the chain tip vs a reference zcashd. 3) Hunt: for every host seen running zebrad, run the 'bad-blk-sigops' log-reject hunt and cross-check the inventory UC to build the full affected-asset list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "zebrad" or FileName =~ "zebrad.exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "zebrad"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
